description: This figure group is composite: a rendered table plus a three-part two-dimensional lattice schematic illustrating solid-solution formation and lattice distortion in iron-based alloys. The table has a header row "Iron base alloy" listing Fe, Mn, Al, Be, C. The row "Atomic size (pm)" gives 124, 124, 143, 111, 77 respectively; the row "Solid solution type" gives "_" for Fe, "Substitution solid solution" for Mn, Al and Be, and "Interstitial solid solution" for C. The schematic below shows three square Fe lattices of green spheres joined by grid lines. Left: a small blue sphere labelled "Be" occupies a substitutional site and the neighbouring lattice lines are bent inward, depicting lattice distortion/shrinkage. Middle: a larger orange sphere labelled "Al" occupies a substitutional site and bows the surrounding planes outward, depicting expansion. Right: a close-packed array of large green spheres labelled "Fe" with small purple spheres labelled "C" sitting in the interstitial gaps. Together the panels argue that Mn, Al and Be dissolve substitutionally whereas C dissolves interstitially, and that Be (smaller than Fe) and Al (larger than Fe) produce opposite lattice distortions. The schematics carry no scale bars or numeric labels.

subfigures.description: Rendered table. Header row 'Iron base alloy' with element columns Fe, Mn, Al, Be, C; 'Atomic size (pm)' row = 124, 124, 143, 111, 77; 'Solid solution type' row = '_' (Fe), 'Substitution solid solution' (Mn), 'Substitution solid solution' (Al), 'Substitution solid solution' (Be), 'Interstitial solid solution' (C).

Two-dimensional square Fe lattice of green spheres with a small blue sphere labelled 'Be' on a substitutional site; the surrounding lattice lines are bent inward, indicating lattice shrinkage/distortion around the undersized solute. Arrows label 'Fe' and 'Be'.

Two-dimensional square Fe lattice with a larger orange sphere labelled 'Al' on a substitutional site; the surrounding lattice lines bow outward, indicating lattice expansion around the oversized solute. Arrows label 'Fe' and 'Al'.
Close-packed array of large green spheres labelled 'Fe' with small purple spheres labelled 'C' located in the interstitial gaps between the Fe spheres; an arrow labels 'C'.

observations.observation: The table header row 'Iron base alloy' lists the elements Fe, Mn, Al, Be and C.
Atomic size (pm) values printed in the table are Fe 124, Mn 124, Al 143, Be 111 and C 77.
The table assigns 'Substitution solid solution' to Mn, Al and Be, 'Interstitial solid solution' to C, and '-' to the Fe base.
The left schematic places a small blue 'Be' sphere on a substitutional Fe lattice site with the grid lines bent inward, depicting lattice shrinkage.
The middle schematic places a larger orange 'Al' sphere on a substitutional Fe lattice site with the grid lines bowed outward, depicting lattice expansion.
The right schematic shows small purple 'C' spheres occupying interstitial gaps between close-packed large green 'Fe' spheres.

The caption states the figure gives the atomic dimensions of elements in steels and the type of solid solution in iron-based alloys (Fig. 18: type of solid solution formed by Mn, Al, C, Be and Fe in steels).
The citing text states that the atomic radius of Be is smaller than that of Fe, so substitutional dissolution causes lattice distortion in which surrounding Fe atoms move closer to the Be atom.
The citing text states that the Al atomic radius is larger than that of Fe, so Al crowds out the surrounding Fe atoms, giving a lattice distortion different from that of Be.

The citing text states that a larger atomic-radius difference gives higher lattice distortion energy and a more unstable lattice, leading to a solubility limit and formation of a Be–Fe phase/Be compound.
The citing text states that Al causes the lattice to expand outward and effectively reduces steel density, whereas Be causes inward lattice expansion and cannot effectively reduce density.
